steps.example: Chapter 1 ended with a purely actual actualizer, chapter 4 with subsistent existence itself — each a description with real content, not a bare placeholder.
steps.challenge: Why take the conclusions of five contested arguments as data at all?
steps.answer: This chapter is conditional on the earlier chapters, which defended each proof at length; its question is what follows if they succeed. Chapter 7 then answers general objections.

steps.example: You get $20 from me because I hand you a bill (formally), wire it from my account (virtually), or have one printed on a press I control (eminently).
steps.challenge: Sponge cake is spongy though no ingredient is, so effects can contain what causes lack.
steps.answer: The ingredients aren’t the total cause; the baker, the mixing, and the heat also count, and the feature may be in the total cause virtually rather than formally.

steps.example: If a $20 bill appeared in your hand with no wallet, account, or press behind it, a potential would be actualized by nothing and the event would have no explanation.
steps.challenge: Explaining an effect by saying its features were “potentially” present makes PPC trivially true (Cottingham).
steps.answer: Explanations by potentialities may be minimally informative but aren’t empty; naturalists like Churchland and their dualist critics draw substantive conclusions from PPC.

steps.example: Plants take in nutrients, grow, and reproduce because they are alive; a stone can’t, and anything that could wouldn’t be a stone.
steps.challenge: A puppet’s wooden limbs dance, which goes beyond the nature of wood.
steps.answer: The principle concerns what a thing does on its own; the puppet’s limbs move only because the puppeteer moves them.

steps.example: “Dog” of Fido and Rover (univocal); “bat” of a mammal and a club (equivocal); “good” of wine and of George (analogical).
steps.challenge: Analogy is just a polite name for metaphor, so analogical talk isn’t literally true.
steps.answer: Metaphor is only one kind of analogy (improper proportionality); attribution and proper proportionality are literal — plants and angels really are alive.

steps.example: An ice cube on hot pavement is actually solid and actually made of water; that actual nature explains why it melts rather than burns.
steps.challenge: Heraclitus: only flux is real; nothing is stably actual.
steps.answer: Then there’d be no persisting reasoner and no stable argument; change is always toward new actualities; and things change according to what they actually are.

steps.example: A sleeping pianist really can play — she differs now from someone who has never learned — though she isn’t playing.
steps.challenge: Parmenides: potentiality is unreal, because change is an illusion.
steps.answer: Denying potency means denying change, which chapter 1 showed cannot coherently be done — even the passing experience of the illusion is a change.

steps.example: Knowing what a dodo is doesn’t tell you whether any dodo exists: essence (potency) and existence (act) are really distinct in creatures.
steps.challenge: Act and potency are just two ways of describing one thing.
steps.answer: Then that one thing would be only actual or only potential, which amounts to denying step 6 or step 7.

steps.example: If the pianist’s ability were real in exactly the way her actual playing is, being able to play would just be playing.
steps.challenge: Why not say potency and act are both simply “real,” full stop?
steps.answer: Sameness of sense would make potency a kind of actuality or vice versa, erasing the real distinction secured at step 8.

steps.example: A baseball bat is a “bat” only in a sense unrelated to the mammal — which is to say it isn’t a mammal-bat at all.
steps.challenge: Maybe potency is real in its own wholly different sense.
steps.answer: Being “real” in a sense with nothing in common with the ordinary sense just means being unreal.

steps.example: Every literal use of “good” is either the same sense, an unrelated sense, or a related-but-different sense; there is no fourth option.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t there be some further kind of literal usage?
steps.answer: Univocal and equivocal are the two extremes (identical vs. unrelated), and analogy covers everything in between, so the three exhaust the options.

steps.example: A man’s existence is to his essence as an angel’s is to its essence and God’s to his — proportionally similar relations, grounding one analogical concept of being.
steps.challenge: This is special pleading invented to rescue theology.
steps.answer: The argument uses only act-potency theory, which one can accept without accepting any proof of God, so it is independently motivated.

steps.example: “God has power” is true, but not in the sense that God has muscles or a will that effortfully overcomes resistance.
steps.challenge: If our words don’t apply in the same sense, we don’t know what we mean when we speak of God.
steps.answer: Analogical concepts are indeterminate, not empty: we affirm a real perfection and deny the limits it has in us; otherwise we could not even say that God exists.

steps.example: The hand-stick-stone series needs a first member that moves without being moved; that member’s existence can’t await actualization.
steps.challenge: Perhaps the regress simply has no first member.
steps.answer: In a hierarchical series each member acts only by borrowed causal power, so without a first member nothing would act at all (chapter 1).

steps.example: Water’s behavior flows from what water is; a being whose very existence is pure act has nothing from which merely potential activity could flow.
steps.challenge: Why can’t something purely actual in existence still have unrealized options in its activity?
steps.answer: Existence is what is most fundamental in a thing and activity follows it; potency for activity would need a source in the nature, and there is none.

steps.example: A lamp that has always been lit still needs the current flowing now; everlasting duration doesn’t explain why the parts are joined.
steps.challenge: A composite that always existed needs no cause.
steps.answer: The issue is ontological, not temporal priority: something must account for the parts being combined at all, and a first cause with a cause isn’t first.

steps.example: The Unmoved Mover not only exists without being actualized; it also acts without any of its activity being actualized by anything.
Two identical pennies differ by their metal (matter); a penny and a dime differ by an added specific difference within the genus coin.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t two things differ in some other way, such as location?
steps.answer: Location presupposes material parts and potency; any genuine intrinsic difference brings composition, and footnote 17 rules out substance/accident parts too.

steps.example: The bronze of a statue could have become a bell; the genus animal is, of itself, open to being rational or nonrational.
steps.challenge: Parts that have always been united have no unrealized potency.
steps.answer: Parts only potentially compose a whole until their union is actualized, and that remains true even if the union had no temporal beginning.

steps.example: Pure act has neither matter to individuate it nor a genus to be specified — there is nothing to add or to receive.
Unlike Zeus, who would still be one god among a possible many even if alone on Olympus, God couldn’t have a rival even in principle.
steps.challenge: Maybe there just happens to be one God, but there could have been more.
steps.answer: Feser’s conclusion is stronger: nothing could distinguish a second purely actual being, so monotheism is true in principle, not by accident.

steps.example: The Unmoved Mover (ch. 1) and the One (ch. 2) turn out to be a single reality described by its lack of potency and its lack of parts.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t something be simple yet have some potential?
steps.answer: Then it would have an actual aspect and a potential aspect — two constituents — and so not be simple after all.

steps.example: A dodo’s essence needs existence added; a being whose essence is existence needs nothing added and so has no potency to be actualized.
steps.challenge: Why can’t the purely actual have an essence distinct from existence?
steps.answer: Where essence and existence differ they relate as potency to act (ch. 4), so such a being would not be purely actual.

steps.example: A simple being can’t be “essence plus existence”; and existence itself can’t be “existence plus anything else,” since that would bring in potency.
You exist contingently because your essence had to be joined to existence by causes; a being with no parts and no potency has nothing that could fail to be supplied.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t a simple, purely actual being just happen to exist, contingently?
steps.answer: Contingency means depending on some potential being actualized or parts being combined; a being with neither can’t exist contingently.

steps.example: Like “morning star” and “evening star” both naming Venus, the five proofs’ descriptions pick out one referent (a course analogy).
steps.challenge: Why not five ultimate beings, one per proof?
steps.answer: The descriptions entail one another and pure actuality entails uniqueness, so all five pick out the one purely actual being.

steps.example: Human rationality and animality can exist apart, so something must combine them; if God’s wisdom and power were distinct, something would have to combine them too.
steps.challenge: Why assume distinct attributes need something to unite them?
steps.answer: A whole of distinct parts is only potentially that whole until its union is actualized (ch. 2); so a God of parts would depend on a uniting cause.

steps.example: Zeus and Odin would keep their natures even as sole occupants of Olympus and Asgard; a composite God would be such a figure, a superangel.
steps.challenge: Isn’t it uncharitable to call theists who reject simplicity implicit atheists?
steps.answer: The claim concerns implications, not sincerity: a composite being would need a cause and so wouldn’t be the ultimate First Cause the proofs conclude to.

steps.example: When Plato grows, Socrates becomes shorter than Plato without any change in Socrates; when the world begins, God becomes Creator without change in God.
steps.challenge: Being Creator is a contingent property of God, so God has contingent properties (Morris).
steps.answer: He has contingent Cambridge properties, not contingent real ones; simplicity identifies only God’s real properties (Miller, building on Geach).

steps.example: Our concepts of God’s power and knowledge are distinct, but they apply analogically to one undivided reality, not to two parts of God.
steps.challenge: Simplicity makes God one property and therefore an abstract object (Plantinga).
steps.answer: That follows only on univocity and Platonic properties; classical theists hold a constituent ontology and never say God is a property.

steps.example: Coffee heating up is its potential for heat being actualized.
steps.challenge: Is all change really actualization of potential, or just rearrangement?
steps.answer: Chapter 1 argued that even rearrangement is a case of potential (to be arranged otherwise) becoming actual.

steps.example: A being with no unrealized capacities has nothing that could become actual, so nothing about it could change.
A leaf turns from green to red while remaining the same leaf: something stays and something goes, which requires parts.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t a simple thing change all at once, entirely?
steps.answer: Total replacement wouldn’t be the thing changing but one thing ceasing and another beginning; real change needs a subject that persists through it.

steps.example: The world’s coming to be is a real change in the world; “God is Creator” becomes true without anything new in God.
steps.challenge: Creating is like Socrates causing Plato to grow, which involves change in Socrates.
steps.answer: That assumes the changes we undergo when acting must occur in every agent — a fallacy of accident (footnote 32).

steps.example: Every professor so far has been under nine feet tall, but no possible professor has to be; likewise every agent we know changes, but acting doesn’t require it.
steps.challenge: When I type, my fingers and brain change; acting always changes the agent.
steps.answer: What is essential to acting is producing an effect in another (Davies); life is acting from an internal principle, which God does most fully.

steps.example: God acts on everything and is acted on by nothing — unlike animals, which must eat and breathe.
steps.challenge: An unchanging God would be frozen and lifeless.
steps.answer: Things change because they lack something; God lacks nothing, and acting from oneself without dependence is life in the fullest sense.

steps.example: Bronze can become a statue or a bell; underneath, prime matter is sheer potency for form.
steps.challenge: Hylomorphism is outdated metaphysics.
steps.answer: Feser gives a second argument (step 38) that doesn’t depend on it.

steps.example: A chair’s legs, a dog’s organs, molecules, atoms — all rearrangeable; even an electron has mass, charge, and spin, and can be created or annihilated.
steps.challenge: Fundamental particles aren’t made of smaller particles, so they are simple.
steps.answer: They still have distinct attributes (parts in a broad sense) and come into being and pass away, which shows potentiality.

steps.example: Whether you picture matter as form plus matter or as particles and fields, it has distinguishable aspects and can be otherwise.
God can’t be a cosmic energy or field, since those are physical realities with attributes and changing states.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t God be some very fine, invisible kind of matter?
steps.answer: Any matter, however fine, is composite and potential, so it would need a cause rather than being the First Cause.

steps.example: A tree begins when its matter and form — and its essence and existence — are joined by causes; before that it was only potential.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t something just pop into existence uncaused?
steps.answer: That would be an actualization with no actualizer and no explanation, against PC and PSR.

steps.example: Existence itself doesn’t need existence added to it, so there’s nothing a cause could supply to it.
steps.challenge: Maybe God began to exist without a cause.
steps.answer: What begins has parts needing combination and is contingent; God has no parts, is necessary, and just is existence, so he couldn’t begin.

steps.example: A tree ends when its parts come apart; subsistent existence has no parts to separate and can hardly lose existence.
God neither comes into being nor passes away — eternity at least in this minimal sense.
steps.challenge: Isn’t that just saying God is very old?
steps.answer: It is only the first stage; steps 45–47 show God’s eternity is timelessness, not endless duration.

steps.example: A temporal God would learn “it is now noon,” then “it is now 12:01,” and keep adding moments to his life.
steps.challenge: God could be in time without changing in any important way.
steps.answer: Any succession — new moments, different acts, new knowledge — is change, and God is immutable; even Craig grants an immutable God would be timeless.

steps.example: God-on-Monday and God-on-Tuesday would be distinct stages of a life — temporal parts.
Like an author who conceives a whole story in one flash, God by one act causes a world in which things exist at t1, t2, t3 (Barr).
steps.challenge: If God causes things at t1 and t2, he acts at t1 and t2 (Swinburne, Pike).
steps.answer: “God causes X to exist at t1” doesn’t entail “at t1 God causes X” (Davies); and eternity isn’t a point in time, so the simultaneity objection fails.

steps.example: You could fail to exist because your existence depended on causes joining an essence to existence.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t something be contingent without having parts or potency?
steps.answer: Contingency just is dependence of existence on some potency’s actualization or some parts’ combination; remove those and nothing remains to depend.

steps.example: The being whose essence is existence has no unactualized potency and no parts that could fail to be combined.
Water can be boiled because of what water is; possibility is grounded in essence, not read off imagined scenarios.
steps.challenge: I can imagine a world with nothing in it, so God might not exist (Schrader).
steps.answer: God, like numbers, can’t be pictured, so imagining absence is irrelevant; and modal truths come from essences, so the objection assumes the proofs fail.

steps.example: God exists in every possible world, not by definition but because of the nature the proofs uncovered: pure act, simplicity, essence identical to existence.
steps.challenge: Necessity belongs only to statements, by linguistic convention (Findlay, Russell).
steps.answer: Propositions aren’t sentences, mathematical necessity isn’t conventional, and the objection begs the question against the proofs’ extralinguistic account of God’s necessity.
